Feeling Mind Controlled Robotic Arm

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
... a robotic arm has been fitted with sensors so the person operating the arm can feel what it is touching.

Unique Selling Point:
Amazing medical technology breakthrough

Summary:
Imagine being in an accident that leaves you unable to feel any sensation in your arms and fingers. Now imagine regaining that sensation, a decade later, through a mind-controlled robotic arm that is directly connected to your brain. This is exactly what scientists at Pittsburgh medical center achieved.

Further information:
BRAIN CHIPS LET A PARALYZED MAN FEEL TOUCH THROUGH A ROBOTIC ARM
The brain chips zap the patient's brain to let him feel when robotic fingers are touched

Nathan Copeland hasn’t been able to move his legs or hands since he broke his neck in a car accident more than a decade ago. But now that scientists have implanted four chips in his brain, Copeland can control a robotic arm with his mind and feel when someone touches its fingers. This is the first time that a neural implant has allowed a person to feel touch through a prosthetic by directly stimulating his brain.
"IT FELT LIKE I WAS GETTING MY FINGERS TOUCHED OR PUSHED."
"It worked great," Copeland says in a video released by the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (UPMC). "It felt like I was getting my fingers touched or pushed." This success — published today in the journal Science Translational Medicine — could help scientists create prosthetics that approximate the way our bodies integrate touch and movement when we grip, grab, and squeeze obects.
Copeland’s life changed when he was 18 years old. He was driving home to Dunbar, Pennsylvania on a rainy night when he rounded a corner too quickly. His seat belt ripped from its moorings, and the crash injured his spinal cord — leaving him paralyzed from the chest down. He can lift his wrists, but he’s lost a lot of the feeling in his fingers and he can’t move them. In 2015, when Copeland was 27, scientists at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center implanted four minuscule arrays of electrodes in his brain. Two of the arrays went into the brain region that governs movement, called the motor cortex. These allow Copeland to control a robotic arm just by thinking about it. (The robotic arm is part of the laboratory, and not attached to Copeland’s body.)
Brain control of a prosthetic’s movements is astounding — but this team of researchers, and others, have done it before. Today’s study differs from previous research in its inclusion of another brain region. The researchers, in fact, implanted two additional arrays — each just 16 square millimeters of electrodes — into the part of Copeland’s brain responsible for sensation, called the sensory cortex.
The research team used brain imaging to figure out exactly which part of the sensory cortex to stick the electrodes in. They watched brain activity as Copeland’s fingers were stroked with cotton swabs, as he watched a video of someone else’s fingers being stroked, and while he imagined someone touching each of his fingers. Together, the images formed a map telling the researchers where to implant the electrodes. These electrodes connected to an outside computer via cables plugged into a socket in Copeland’s skull. The computer was in turn linked to the sensors in the robotic arm. When someone touched one of the robotic fingers, the sensors relayed that information to the computer, which then told the electrodes to zap Copeland’s sensory cortex.
It took a full month for Copeland to start feeling anything more than tingling in his right arm. That’s because the researchers didn’t know how well the system would work, so they started stimulating Copeland’s brain with very low levels of electricity at first — increasing the intensity incrementally over time. "When it did start to work as expected, it was a big relief," says Jennifer Collinger, a bioengineer at the University of Pittsburgh and a co-author of the study. And it kept working, for the entire six months that the study continued.

THE ELECTRODES ZAP COPELAND'S SENSORY CORTEX
These results are impressive, and a much needed step for developing the next generation of prosthetics, says Bolu Ajiboye, a biomedical engineer at Case Western Reserve University who was not involved in the study. In the future, the technology could help design prosthetics that can automatically adjust their grip based on the object — just like our bodies do instinctively when we grab an egg versus, say, a doorknob. "We don’t talk about this part of movement, but to actually be able to move naturally, you need sensory feedback," he says. "Think about holding a newborn. If you don’t have sensory feedback you don’t know how much force to use when you’re holding a child."
Though today’s research is a big step, it’ll be a while before paralyzed people outside of a research laboratory will be able to use brain implants to feel touch through a prosthetic. Scientists still don’t fully understand how electrical stimulation of the sensory cortex corresponds to the sense of touch. So more research is needed. "The science on the sensory side is very rudimentary," says Andrew Schwartz, a neurophysiologist at the University of Pittsburgh and a co-author of the study.
"IF YOU DON’T HAVE SENSORY FEEDBACK YOU DON’T KNOW HOW MUCH FORCE TO USE"
The implant itself is still being evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration, which has to approve new medical devices. (The researchers were allowed to use it for clinical research under an FDA exemption, but they have to keep applying for an extension every year.) Researchers also need to figure out a way to integrate the cables, wires, and robotic arm into the patient’s body. Right now, the arm is separate, the cables are massive, and the system requires large, desk-bound computers.
As for Copeland, he has a clear vision for lifelike prosthetics that seamlessly integrate sensation and movement — because he’s seen one before. "Luke Skywalker got his hand chopped off, and the next day he has a robot one. And they’re pricking it, and he’s like, ‘Yeah I can feel it. Good to go’ — and he doesn’t even miss a beat," he says in the video. "That could be someone else — not even that far in the future."

Press Release:


Imagine being in an accident that renders you quadriplegic and unable to feel any sensation in your arms and fingers. Now imagine regaining that sensation,
a decade later, through a mind-controlled robotic arm that is directly connected to your brain. Carte Blanche meets the researchers who’ve developed a
remarkable robotic arm that’s not only controlled by the mind, but also allows the operator to actually feel what they are touching.

Script:


V/O:
Former United States President Barack Obama has shaken many hands in his career, but this one was one of the strangest. A handshake with a robotic arm. But what is even more remarkable is that 30-year-old Nathan Copeland could feel the grip as if it were his own hand.

Nathan was paralyzed from the chest down in a car accident 10 years ago.
5

13

4
Nathan:
Lots of things are hard – picking cups up. Regaining the ability to do things can really change someone’s life.
V/O:
His life changed at the University of Pittsburgh when he met Professors Mike Boninger and Robert Gaunt at a clinical trial involving an amazing mind controlled robotic arm.
12
LINK 1:
They told him about the trial and that they needed a volunteer to undergo brain surgery to link his mind to the robotic arm. For him it held the promise of one day being more independent.
13
Rob Gaunt:
We have a robotic arm and with this robotic arm we can take devices that we have implanted in the brain and a person can reach out with this robotic arm and grabs objects and feel when they contact it. They can feel with the robotic hand.
V/O:
Prof Gaunt’s field of speciality is brain stimulation and the robotic arm they use is a copy of the robotic arm we featured on Carte Blanche last year. The Advanced Physics Lab at Johns Hopkins University had shown it was possible to control the arm through thought alone as this man is doing here.

The research team at Pittsburgh ordered such an arm for their own research. They wanted to modify it so it could be even more functional.
25
Ou Carte Blanche
LINK 2:
When a copy of this arm arrived in Pittsburgh the first step was to make sure they could also control the arm through thought.
8
V/O:
They advertised for volunteers and the first was Jan Scheuermann who at that stage had been completely paralysed for 10 years. She agreed to undergo brain surgery to test the arm.
9
Mike Boninger:
She was the first person at the University of Pittsburgh where we put tow arrays in the motor part of the brain, the part that controls movement.
V/O:
Prof Mike Boninger is the head of Department of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation at Pittsburgh University.

An array is a tiny device with ninety six small pins, that can be placed onto the surface of the brain, to detect patterns of brain activity. The signals are then sent via connectors on top of the head to a computer.
6

12
Mike:
So when you normally move your hand what happens is that you think “I want to grab something”. You don’t actually think I need to move my hand. You think about an activity you want to do. In a part of the brain cells fire, those cells become a pattern and that patterns goes to nerves in your arm and the arm moves because the nerves in the muscles fire. The nerves carry the signals to the muscles like a wire. In a spinal cord injury that connection is severed, but the activity in the brain is still normal.
LINK 3:
So, when you think about moving your arm or hand or touching something, neurons fire in the brain in a very specific pattern.
7
V/O:
This neural activity can be detected by the arrays and relayed to a computer. The computer then sends signals to the robotic arm that make it move in a certain way. The implants in Jan’s brain worked perfectly.
12

Mike:
Jan was able to control the robotic arm through her thoughts.
Jan:
I can’t stop smiling, it is so cool. I am moving things. I have not moved things for about 10 years.
Mike:
Right now all Jan is doing is imagining the moving arm exactly where she wants it to go. Just like you or I would control our own arm.
LINK 4:
But Jan also wanted to do something very specific with the robotic arm. 5
Jan:
They were asking if there was something specific I would like to like touching my children’s cheek or holding my husband’s hand and I said “my goal is to feed myself chocolate”.
V/O:
And Jan was indeed able to feed herself a chocolate bar to the delight of all around her.
6
LINK 5:
But the team knew that was not enough to be able to just move the arm and hand. Something was missing.
8
V/O:
And what was missing was sensation. It is such an important part of touching. We constantly need sensation to figure out what we are touching and how we are touching something. Jan could see what the hand was touching, but it was not enough. She could not feel anything.
16
Mike:
So very fine dexterous movements of the hand like buttoning your shirt or tying your shoes, vision is not enough. You can’t just watch and do that. You need sensation to be able to control the hand specifically and the arm in general with the type of level of control that you and I have.
V/O:
But how do you let somebody feel what a robotic hand is touching? Prof Gaunt had the answer.
7
Rob:
So one thing that we know is that there is a specific spot in the brain, a strip in the brain called the somatosensory cortex and this is the part of the brain that become active when you touch something, when you move. When you reach and grab something neurons, individual cells in the brain become active and light up.
V/O:
Past brain research has generated a complete map of where in the brain sensations from various parts of the body are processed.
10
Rob:
And in fact there is even a map within the hand. There is a spot in the brain that is the little finger spot and then the fourth finger and the down to the thumb and it is very organized.
LINK 6:
With his expertise in brain stimulation Prof Gaunt knew he could use this map to accomplish something unprecedented.
5
Rob:
But what we also know now is that if you stick electrodes into these particular spots in the brain, if you put a little wire essentially into the part of the brain that normally responds when the thumb is being touched or touches something, and you electrically stimulate it that is you send little tiny pulses of electricity into that part of the brain, a person experiences it as though their own thumb is being touched.
V/O:
To get impulses from the robotic hand to the brain, special sensors were created.
7
Rob:
There’s sensors in various locations in the hand, there are sensors at the motors that drive the fingers. There are also sensors at the tip of each of these fingers. What actually would happen is that we record information from the sensors in the robot and that runs into our computer system and the computer works through this map that we just talked about and figures out which electrodes to stimulate in the brain.
V/O:
To see if this would work in real life, another volunteer was needed and that was where Nathan Copeland came in. The team implanted four arrays into Nathan’s brain – two in the motor cortex so he could control the arm, and two in the sensory cortex so he could receive sensations from the hand. The experiment was a huge success. Not only could Nathan control the arm by thinking but, when the hand touched something, it felt as if he were using his own hand. He could even detect when individual fingers were touched by someone.
29
Nathan:
…..index………………….It is a really weird sensation. Sometimes it feels like kind of electrical and sometimes it is more like a pressure.

V/O:
For the most part Nathan can distinguish fairly well between different fingers when they are touched and can tell when pressure is applied.
8
LINK 7:
The team was delighted, and hope refine the system further so it can one day be even more useful.
4
V/O:
And when a President and a robotic hand exchanged a fist bump last year it highlighted the science fiction-like technology that could one day profoundly change the lives of thousands of people like Nathan.
12

LINK 6: With his expertise in brain stimulation Prof Gaunt knew he could use this map to accomplish something unprecedented. 5 Rob: But what we also know now is that if you stick electrodes into these particular spots in the brain, if you put a little wire essentially into the part of the brain that normally responds when the thumb is being touched or touches something, and you electrically stimulate it that is you send little tiny pulses of electricity into that part of the brain, a person experiences it as though their own thumb is being touched. V/O: To get impulses from the robotic hand to the brain, special sensors were created. 7 Rob: There’s sensors in various locations in the hand, there are sensors at the motors that drive the fingers. There are also sensors at the tip of each of these fingers. What actually would happen is that we record information from the sensors in the robot and that runs into our computer system and the computer works through this map that we just talked about and figures out which electrodes to stimulate in the brain. V/O: To see if this would work in real life, another volunteer was needed and that was where Nathan Copeland came in. The team implanted four arrays into Nathan’s brain – two in the motor cortex so he could control the arm, and two in the sensory cortex so he could receive sensations from the hand. The experiment was a huge success. Not only could Nathan control the arm by thinking but, when the hand touched something, it felt as if he were using his own hand. He could even detect when individual fingers were touched by someone. 29 Nathan: …..index………………….It is a really weird sensation. Sometimes it feels like kind of electrical and sometimes it is more like a pressure. V/O: For the most part Nathan can distinguish fairly well between different fingers when they are touched and can tell when pressure is applied. 8 LINK 7: The team was delighted, and hope refine the system further so it can one day be even more useful. 4 V/O: And when a President and a robotic hand exchanged a fist bump last year it highlighted the science fiction-like technology that could one day profoundly change the lives of thousands of people like Nathan. 12

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): ... a robotic arm has been fitted with sensors so the person operating the arm can feel what it is touching.
metadata.Summary: Imagine being in an accident that leaves you unable to feel any sensation in your arms and fingers. Now imagine regaining that sensation, a decade later, through a mind-controlled robotic arm that is directly connected to your brain. This is exactly what scientists at Pittsburgh medical center achieved.
metadata.Further information: BRAIN CHIPS LET A PARALYZED MAN FEEL TOUCH THROUGH A ROBOTIC ARM The brain chips zap the patient's brain to let him feel when robotic fingers are touched Nathan Copeland hasn’t been able to move his legs or hands since he broke his neck in a car accident more than a decade ago. But now that scientists have implanted four chips in his brain, Copeland can control a robotic arm with his mind and feel when someone touches its fingers. This is the first time that a neural implant has allowed a person to feel touch through a prosthetic by directly stimulating his brain. "IT FELT LIKE I WAS GETTING MY FINGERS TOUCHED OR PUSHED." "It worked great," Copeland says in a video released by the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (UPMC). "It felt like I was getting my fingers touched or pushed." This success — published today in the journal Science Translational Medicine — could help scientists create prosthetics that approximate the way our bodies integrate touch and movement when we grip, grab, and squeeze obects. Copeland’s life changed when he was 18 years old. He was driving home to Dunbar, Pennsylvania on a rainy night when he rounded a corner too quickly. His seat belt ripped from its moorings, and the crash injured his spinal cord — leaving him paralyzed from the chest down. He can lift his wrists, but he’s lost a lot of the feeling in his fingers and he can’t move them. In 2015, when Copeland was 27, scientists at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center implanted four minuscule arrays of electrodes in his brain. Two of the arrays went into the brain region that governs movement, called the motor cortex. These allow Copeland to control a robotic arm just by thinking about it. (The robotic arm is part of the laboratory, and not attached to Copeland’s body.) Brain control of a prosthetic’s movements is astounding — but this team of researchers, and others, have done it before. Today’s study differs from previous research in its inclusion of another brain region. The researchers, in fact, implanted two additional arrays — each just 16 square millimeters of electrodes — into the part of Copeland’s brain responsible for sensation, called the sensory cortex. The research team used brain imaging to figure out exactly which part of the sensory cortex to stick the electrodes in. They watched brain activity as Copeland’s fingers were stroked with cotton swabs, as he watched a video of someone else’s fingers being stroked, and while he imagined someone touching each of his fingers. Together, the images formed a map telling the researchers where to implant the electrodes. These electrodes connected to an outside computer via cables plugged into a socket in Copeland’s skull. The computer was in turn linked to the sensors in the robotic arm. When someone touched one of the robotic fingers, the sensors relayed that information to the computer, which then told the electrodes to zap Copeland’s sensory cortex. It took a full month for Copeland to start feeling anything more than tingling in his right arm. That’s because the researchers didn’t know how well the system would work, so they started stimulating Copeland’s brain with very low levels of electricity at first — increasing the intensity incrementally over time. "When it did start to work as expected, it was a big relief," says Jennifer Collinger, a bioengineer at the University of Pittsburgh and a co-author of the study. And it kept working, for the entire six months that the study continued. THE ELECTRODES ZAP COPELAND'S SENSORY CORTEX These results are impressive, and a much needed step for developing the next generation of prosthetics, says Bolu Ajiboye, a biomedical engineer at Case Western Reserve University who was not involved in the study. In the future, the technology could help design prosthetics that can automatically adjust their grip based on the object — just like our bodies do instinctively when we grab an egg versus, say, a doorknob. "We don’t talk about this part of movement, but to actually be able to move naturally, you need sensory feedback," he says. "Think about holding a newborn. If you don’t have sensory feedback you don’t know how much force to use when you’re holding a child." Though today’s research is a big step, it’ll be a while before paralyzed people outside of a research laboratory will be able to use brain implants to feel touch through a prosthetic. Scientists still don’t fully understand how electrical stimulation of the sensory cortex corresponds to the sense of touch. So more research is needed. "The science on the sensory side is very rudimentary," says Andrew Schwartz, a neurophysiologist at the University of Pittsburgh and a co-author of the study. "IF YOU DON’T HAVE SENSORY FEEDBACK YOU DON’T KNOW HOW MUCH FORCE TO USE" The implant itself is still being evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration, which has to approve new medical devices. (The researchers were allowed to use it for clinical research under an FDA exemption, but they have to keep applying for an extension every year.) Researchers also need to figure out a way to integrate the cables, wires, and robotic arm into the patient’s body. Right now, the arm is separate, the cables are massive, and the system requires large, desk-bound computers. As for Copeland, he has a clear vision for lifelike prosthetics that seamlessly integrate sensation and movement — because he’s seen one before. "Luke Skywalker got his hand chopped off, and the next day he has a robot one. And they’re pricking it, and he’s like, ‘Yeah I can feel it. Good to go’ — and he doesn’t even miss a beat," he says in the video. "That could be someone else — not even that far in the future."
